newsitem.title: USA: Dole to campaign around the clock until election.
newsitem.headline: Dole to campaign around the clock until election.

text.p: In a drastic move to catch up on President Bill Clinton, Republican challenger Bob Dole said on Thursday he would campaign around-the-clock for the last four days before the presidential election, comparing his all-out bid to his Second World War service.
Plans call for the 73-year-old to barnstorm through at least eleven states and possibly as many as 15 in a marathon that may set new standards for gruelling campaign finales.
"The last time I fought round-the-clock for my country was in 1945, in Italy," Dole said in reference to his military service when he was badly wounded.
"I will once again fight round-the-clock for America's future. Ninety-six hours of nonstop campaigning. From noon Friday until noon on Nov. 5," he said.
"I am determined to make every hour of this decisive election count," said Dole. "The stakes are that high."

Dole press secretary Nelson Warfield said the trip would be by bus, plane and possibly other modes of transport with only stops for campaign events, filing time for reporters and an occasional shower.

Others, including losing Democratic candidates George McGovern in 1972 and Michael Dukakis in 1988, have made extensive last-gasp efforts, but the one envisioned by Dole could exceed them for sheer non-stop activity over so long a time and so much territory.
Four years ago, Clinton campaigned nonstop for 30 hours starting in Philadelphia, westward to Denver and ending on election day in Arkansas but that was by plane only.
"This is a fight for America -- to elect a president we can trust and an economy that gives us hope," said Dole. "I will give it all I've got."

"Ninety-six hours. From the factories of Ohio and Michigan, through the bluegrass of Kentucky, in the towns and neighbourhoods of the Midwest, across the Rocky Mountains, through the cities and streets of California," Dole said.
Dole planned to complete campaigning in Florida and then Atlanta before finishing the day in Columbus, Ohio, on Thursday night before the start of his long trip.

All opinion polls show Clinton leading Dole by a comfortable margin. The Reuters tracking poll on Thursday put Clinton ahead by 7.7 points and a new poll in California showed Clinton leading by 18 points.

States that Dole expects to hit are Ohio, Michigan, Kentucky, Missouri, Nebraska, South Dakota, Colorado, Nevada, California, New Mexico and Kansas. Aides said New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Indiana and Tennessee might also be woven in.
During his speech, Dole also told southern Florida's large Cuban-American community that he would oppose Cuba's leader Fidel Castro more than Clinton would.

"I will also be the president who stands up to Fidel Castro's regime and fights for freedom in Cuba," said Dole. "Bill Clinton is a bigger friend of the Castro regime than of the Cuban American community. He's just hoping Cuban-Americans will listen to his rhetoric."

Earlier, former President George Bush pitched in to give Dole a hand. "I believe in keeping the White House above partisan politics and away from these puny, terrible disputes we're seeing," Bush said.

Bush, beaten by Clinton in 1992, in accusing the president of running a partisan White House implicitly referred to controversies over donations to the Democratic Party from people with ties to Indonesia, Taiwan and other foreign interests.
"Bob Dole is the person to lead this country into the next millennium. What it's about is leadership...We need somebody to restore the respect to America around the world," said Bush.
